title: Riders to the Sea
description: The perfect one-act tragedy in English: a mother in the Aran Islands loses her last son to the sea. It is a dramatic work of 1904 by J. M. Synge; it belongs to The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre and it is catalogued here under Peasant Play and the Irish Dramatic Movement; Verse Drama and the Poetic Play and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: Maurya has lost six sons and her husband to the sea; her last son Bartley insists on taking the horses to the mainland fair. While he is gone, the body of her drowned son Michael is brought in, and Bartley is killed when his horse throws him into the sea; the play ends with Maurya's great lament.
narrative_structure: Single act in a cottage kitchen, with the offstage sea as the antagonist. The action is divided into acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts in the spoken Irish idiom, moving between the comic exchange and the elegiac set speech.
principal_characters: Maurya; Bartley; Cathleen; Nora; the young priest; the women at the wake
literary_form: One-act tragedy (first performed at the Abbey Theatre, 25 February 1904)
meter_and_prosody: Dramatic text. Dramatic prose in the Hiberno-English idiom: the syntax and the imagery of the Irish speech are carried into English dialogue, and the play moves between the comic exchange and the elegiac set speech. The text is divided into acts, with the scene changes marked. The author's characteristic manner is a poetic prose built from the actual syntax and idiom of Irish-English speech.
historical_context: The Aran Islands and the fishing economy of the Congested Districts; the keening tradition and the ritual lament of the Irish wake. The record dates the work as composed in 1903 and first published in 1904 and first performed in 1904 and the corpus places it within The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre, it is catalogued under peasant play and the irish dramatic movement; verse drama and the poetic play.
literary_significance: Riders to the Sea is the finest one-act tragedy in English: in twenty minutes it achieves the scale of Greek tragedy, its prose is the most musical in modern drama, and its lament is one of the great passages in Irish writing.

bibliographical_notes: First produced at the Molesworth Hall, Dublin, on 25 February 1904 and published by Elkin Mathews in London and Maunsel in Dublin in 1904. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: The Aran Islands

Synge; it belongs to The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre and it is catalogued here under Documentary Prose and the Reportage Book; Nature Essay and the Rural Observation and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: Synge describes four visits between 1898 and 1902: the cottages, the kelp-making, the fishing, the wakes, the story-tellers and the old men whose speech he transcribes almost phonetically, and his own slow acceptance by the islanders.
narrative_structure: Four parts corresponding to four visits, in diary and descriptive prose. A book of reportage in scenes, each scene observed and transcribed, the argument carried by the sequence rather than by commentary. A series of observations arranged by season or by month, the exact natural-history detail carried in the lyrical sentence.
principal_characters: J. M. Synge, the narrator; old Mourteen, his teacher of Irish; Pat Dirane, the story-teller; Michael, his young guide
literary_form: Travel book (four parts); documentary prose
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of reportage: the observed scene rendered in the present tense or the immediate past, the transcribed speech of the witness, the document quoted in full, and the argument carried by the sequence of scenes. The author's characteristic manner is a poetic prose built from the actual syntax and idiom of Irish-English speech.
historical_context: The Aran Islands and the Congested Districts Board, the last years of the Irish-speaking peasant culture, and the folklore collecting movement. The record dates the work as composed between 1898 and 1902 and first published in 1907 and the corpus places it within The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre, it is catalogued under documentary prose and the reportage book; nature essay and the rural observation.

title: The Shadow of a Gunman
description: The first of O'Casey's Dublin plays: a poet is mistaken for an IRA gunman, with tragic consequences. It is a dramatic work of 1923 by Sean O'Casey; it belongs to The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre and it is catalogued here under Peasant Play and the Irish Dramatic Movement; Comedy of Manners and the Drawing-Room Stage and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: Donal Davoren, a poet sharing a tenement room with the pedlar Seumas Shields, is assumed by the neighbours to be an IRA man on the run. When a raid comes, the innocent Tommy Owens is killed and Davoren's illusions are exposed, in a play that turns from comedy to tragedy in its last minutes.
narrative_structure: Two acts in one tenement room, with the raid as the turning point. The action is divided into two acts, each closing on a discovery or a reversal. A play in acts in the spoken Irish idiom, moving between the comic exchange and the elegiac set speech.

title: Juno and the Paycock

plot_or_argument: The Boyles — the boasting 'Captain' Boyle, his long-suffering wife Juno, their daughter Mary and their son Johnny — are told they have inherited a fortune. They furnish on credit; the inheritance collapses; Mary is pregnant and abandoned; and Johnny, who has betrayed a comrade, is shot and dragged away. The play ends with Juno taking her daughter away and Boyle left alone with his drunken friend Joxer.

title: The Plough and the Stars

title: The Poacher

plot_or_argument: Salar the Salmon follows the salmon from the parr in the river to the sea and the return of the grilse to the pool and the net, in the prose of the water that made Tarka the standard of the nature narrative.
narrative_structure: A nature narrative in chapters of the migration and the return. A series of observations arranged by season or by month, the exact natural-history detail carried in the lyrical sentence.
principal_characters: Salar; the nets; the river; the sea
literary_form: Nature narrative (the life of a salmon)
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the nature essay: the exact observation of the season, the field and the creature, the scientific nomenclature beside the lyrical sentence, and the diary or month-by-month arrangement. The author's characteristic manner is the prose of the wild creature followed hour by hour and season by season.
historical_context: The rivers and the sea of the west country in the 1930s. The record dates the work as composed between 1933 and 1934 and first published in 1935 and it is catalogued under nature essay and the rural observation; provincial novel and the british rural chronicle.
literary_significance: Salar the Salmon is the companion to Tarka and the second of the great nature narratives: its river, its sea and its net carried the prose of the wild creature into the migration and the return.

literary_form: Novel (the young man and the young woman of the republic)

title: Bird Alone
description: The novel of the young man against the church and the state, banned in Ireland. It is a prose fiction work of 1936 by Sean O'Faolain; it is catalogued here under Novel of Development and the Growth Story; Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: Bird Alone follows Corney Cassidy from the civil war to the Dublin of the censorship, against the church, the state and the family, in the first person of the young man alone; the book was banned in Ireland in the year of its publication.
narrative_structure: A novel in the first person, in chapters from the civil war to the alone. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult. A novel organised by the movement of consciousness rather than by chronology: long unbroken passages of thought, time-shifts and repetitions, with the external action reported from inside a single mind.
principal_characters: Corney Cassidy; the family; the priests; the women of the city
literary_form: Novel (the young man against the church and the state)
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose fiction of formation: the narrative follows one consciousness from childhood or youth to settlement, in chapters grouped by the stages of the life, with the earlier manner recalled and judged by the later. The author's characteristic manner is the short story of the civil war and the censorship in the plain ironic sentence.
historical_context: Ireland from the civil war to the 1930s, and the censored book. The record dates the work as composed between 1934 and 1935 and first published in 1936 and it is catalogued under novel of development and the growth story; novel of consciousness and the stream of mind.
literary_significance: Bird Alone is O'Faolain's masterpiece and one of the great censored books of Ireland: its Corney Cassidy alone against the church and the state made the novel of the republic a national text and its banning a national scandal.
